job: Differential fluid service (one axle, drain and refill)
unit: per axle: one drain and refill of a single differential (the rear differential on the examples) with the maker-specified fluid, bought in whole quarts to cover the capacity shown for each example, plus new drain-plug and fill-plug washers where the maker calls for them. Not included: the second axle on a four-wheel-drive or all-wheel-drive vehicle, the transfer case, limited-slip friction modifier, removing and resealing an axle cover on axles with no drain plug, repeat drain-and-refills, seals, or diagnosis of a noise or leak

finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to grade; these are first figures. Shops usually sell a differential service at a set menu price, not as parts plus clocked labor. Built totals for ONE axle (fluid and washers + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2023 Honda HR-V AWD about $96-$190 (2 quarts of Honda DPSF-II for a 1.32 qt change; washers not costed); midsize 2023 Honda CR-V AWD about $98-$193 (2 quarts plus two plug washers); luxury 2018 Acura MDX about $98-$193 (2 quarts of Acura DPSF for a 1.92 qt change, plus two washers); truck 2016 Ford F-150 rear axle about $152-$250 (3 quarts of Motorcraft 75W-85 for a 5.5 pint fill). A fair plain-language range is roughly $95-$195 for one differential on a car or crossover and $150-$250 for a full-size truck axle; a vehicle with front and rear differentials roughly doubles it. Against the benchmarks: the car totals cover Jerry's $100-$200, RepairPal's national $144-$179 and the top of FIXD's $79-$93; YourMechanic's Crosstrek figure ($169-$189) sits near the top of the car range. RepairPal's own Honda CR-V figure ($81-$109) is at or just below our floor, and its F-150 figure ($197-$232) sits inside the truck range. How solid the figures are, stated plainly. Capacities are the strongest part: all four come from maker documents (Honda's online owner's manuals, an Acura service bulletin, and Ford's 2016 F-150 owner's manual read on a manual-hosting site, backed by Ford's own Motorcraft axle chart). Labor is weaker: the 0.6 hr low end for every class is one manufacturer time, GM's 'Drain and Fill Rear Axle Fluid' 0.6 hr for 2021-2024 full-size GM sport utilities, which is none of the example vehicles; the 1.0 hr high end is a lubricant maker's do-it-yourself guide, with a second lubricant maker's guide at 45 minutes in between. No Honda, Acura or Ford time for the fluid service alone was found: the Honda and Acura bulletins loaded print 0.7 hr for a pump motor replacement that includes draining and refilling the differential, which supports a fluid-only time under 0.7 hr on the MDX and Pilot but is not a fluid-only time. The truck hours assume a drain and refill; a truck axle with no drain plug needs the cover removed and resealed or the oil suctioned out, which can take longer and adds a gasket or sealant that is not costed. Prices: the three Honda-family lows are the genuine fluid at a dealer's discounted price, not an aftermarket fluid, because none stated to meet the Honda specification loaded with a price; the F-150 low and high are both retailer prices for the genuine Motorcraft fluid (no Ford list price loaded, and the higher-priced page showed the item out of stock). Three of the four examples share one fluid, so the car classes barely differ; vehicles that use ordinary 75W-90 gear oil (Subaru, Toyota, most trucks) can cost less in fluid, and limited-slip axles that need friction modifier cost more. The model years of the HR-V and CR-V manual pages are taken from their publication codes, not printed on the pages, and the F-150 capacity was matched by position in a table that loaded with labels and values separated. An estimate is not a quote. Posted menu prices loaded on 2026-11-20 from eight sellers' own pages (six dealers, one regional chain and one local multi-shop independent in New Jersey, Ohio, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Louisiana, Georgia, North Carolina and Kentucky) run from $79.95 to $179.95 for one axle, mostly before tax and shop fees, which sits inside the $95-$195 built for a car: $79.95-$89.95 at a Subaru dealer, $99.99 at the chain, $114.95 at a Toyota dealer, $129.95-$179.95 at four Honda dealers and $170.25-$174.41 at the independent; national chains were not searched because they do not print this price.
extras: A quote often adds shop supplies, gear oil disposal and sales tax. A four-wheel-drive or all-wheel-drive vehicle has a second differential and usually a transfer case, each priced separately or bundled as a driveline service. Limited-slip axles may need a friction modifier additive, and some trucks specify a costlier 75W-140 synthetic oil. Axles with no drain plug need the cover removed and a new gasket or sealant, which adds time and parts. If the visit is for a whine, clunk or leak, expect a diagnosis fee, and seals, bearings or a pinion repair are quoted separately. Trucks used for towing are often advised to change the fluid more often.
